title: Given a list of intervals each with a start and an end, merge all overlapping intervals and return the list of non-overlapping intervals that cover the same ranges. Solve it with the sort-then-sweep merge-intervals pattern and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.

s1_definition.profdef: The merge intervals problem asks to combine any intervals that overlap or touch into single continuous intervals, producing a minimal set of non-overlapping intervals covering the same ranges. It is solved by sorting the intervals by start value and then sweeping left to right, extending the current merged interval whenever the next interval's start is within the current end, otherwise closing the current interval and starting a new one. It runs in n log n time dominated by the sort.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh has a list of time windows during which various account-maintenance locks were held, and some windows overlap. He wants to collapse them into the minimal set of distinct locked periods. He first lines the windows up by their start times, then walks through them, stretching the current locked period whenever the next window begins before the current one ends, and starting a fresh period whenever there is a clean gap.
s1_definition.oneliner: Sort by start, then sweep, extending the current interval when the next start is within the current end, else start a new one.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The merge intervals problem asks to combine any intervals that overlap or touch into single continuous intervals, producing a minimal set of non-overlapping intervals covering the same ranges. It is solved by sorting the intervals by start value and then sweeping left to right, extending the current merged interval whenever the next interval's start is within the current end, otherwise closing the current interval and starting a new one. It runs in n log n time dominated by the sort.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, Rajesh has a list of time windows during which various account-maintenance locks were held, and some windows overlap. He wants to collapse them into the minimal set of distinct locked periods. He first lines the windows up by their start times, then walks through them, stretching the current locked period whenever the next window begins before the current one ends, and starting a fresh period whenever there is a clean gap.

**One line to remember:** Sort by start, then sweep, extending the current interval when the next start is within the current end, else start a new one.

sections.s2_technical:
The decisive first step is sorting the intervals by their start value. Once sorted, any interval that overlaps with an earlier one must overlap with the most recently merged interval, because everything is in start order, so we never need to look backward more than one step. This sorting is what turns a potentially complicated overlap problem into a simple single sweep.

After sorting we initialize the current merged interval as the first interval. For each subsequent interval we compare its start to the current merged interval's end. If the next start is less than or equal to the current end, the two overlap or touch, so we merge by extending the current end to the maximum of the current end and the next end, written `curEnd = Math.max(curEnd, next.end)`. We take the maximum because the next interval might end before the current one, in which case it is fully contained and the current end should not shrink. If instead the next start is strictly greater than the current end, there is a gap, so we finalize the current merged interval by adding it to the result and begin a new current interval at the next one.

A decision point is whether intervals that merely touch, where the next start equals the current end, should be merged. In most banking scenarios touching windows represent a continuous period and should be combined, so we use less than or equal to rather than strictly less than. After the loop we must remember to add the final current interval to the result, because the last merged interval is only closed out when a gap appears or the loop ends, and the loop ending is easy to forget. The senior-level nuance is exactly this pair of details, taking the maximum of the ends and flushing the final interval.

We do not mutate the input; we build a fresh result list. The time complexity is n log n dominated by the sort, with the sweep itself linear, and the space complexity is O(n) for the sorted copy and the result, or O(1) extra beyond the output if we sort in place. This sort-then-sweep template is the foundation of the entire merge-intervals family of problems.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, the account-maintenance system records time windows during which exclusive locks were held on an account for various operations, and these windows frequently overlap because several operations run concurrently. The audit team wants to collapse the overlapping windows into the minimal set of distinct continuous locked periods, because the regulator asks for the actual total time an account was under any lock, not a raw list of overlapping entries. This is exactly the merge intervals problem.

Problem 2 — Comparing every window against every other to find overlaps is quadratic and does not scale for busy accounts with many lock entries. Sorting by start and sweeping once collapses all overlaps in n log n time, which keeps the audit-report generation fast.

The code has the shared `Account` class, an `Interval` class representing a lock window, a `LockWindowMerger` service with a `mergeLockedPeriods` method implementing sort-then-sweep, and a runnable `MergeIntervalsDemo` main class that merges Rajesh's and Priya's lock windows, logging each merge or new interval at fine level and the merged list at info level.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's lock windows are [1,3], [2,6], [8,10], [15,18]. First we sort by start, which leaves them in the same order since they are already sorted. We initialize the current merged interval as start 1, end 3.

Step 1: Next is [2,6]. Its start 2 is less than or equal to the current end 3, so they overlap. We extend the current end to the maximum of 3 and 6, which is 6. Current is now start 1, end 6.

Step 2: Next is [8,10]. Its start 8 is greater than the current end 6, so there is a gap. We finalize the current interval [1,6] into the result and start a new current at start 8, end 10.

Step 3: Next is [15,18]. Its start 15 is greater than the current end 10, so there is a gap. We finalize [8,10] into the result and start a new current at start 15, end 18.

After the loop we flush the final current interval [15,18] into the result.

The merged locked periods for Rajesh are [1,6], [8,10], [15,18].

```
    ├─ [2,6]  start2 ≤ end3  → extend end=max(3,6)=6  cur=[1,6]

  Output: [[1,6],[8,10],[15,18]]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The merge intervals problem asks me to collapse any overlapping or touching intervals into a minimal set of non-overlapping intervals covering the same ranges, and I solve it with a sort-then-sweep in n log n time. The decisive step is sorting by start value, because once the intervals are in start order, any interval that overlaps an earlier one must overlap the most recently merged interval, so I never look back more than one step. That ordering is what turns a messy overlap problem into a single clean sweep.

After sorting I keep a current merged interval and walk the rest. If the next interval's start is at or before the current end, they overlap or touch, so I extend the current end to the maximum of the current end and the next end, taking the maximum because the next interval might be fully contained and I must not shrink the current end. If the next start is beyond the current end there is a gap, so I finalize the current interval and start a new one. The two details I always call out are taking the maximum of the ends and flushing the final current interval after the loop, since the last interval is only closed out by a gap that may never come.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in the account-maintenance system. We recorded time windows during which exclusive locks were held on an account for concurrent operations, and these windows frequently overlapped, but the regulator asked for the actual total time an account was under any lock, not a raw overlapping list. Sorting the windows by start and sweeping once collapsed all overlaps into the minimal set of distinct locked periods in n log n time, which kept audit-report generation fast even for busy accounts.

The senior-level point I make is that sorting by start is the enabling move for the entire merge-intervals family, and that almost every harder interval problem, like inserting an interval, finding intersections, or scheduling meeting rooms, builds on this same sort-and-sweep skeleton. I also stress the maximum-of-ends rule for contained intervals and the easily forgotten final flush, since those are the two places correctness slips, and I mention deciding deliberately whether touching intervals merge, which is a domain choice. Framing this as the base template for a whole category, plus naming the two subtle correctness details, is what tells an interviewer I understand it as a pattern rather than a one-off.
